canonical_topic: Compression heating, cooling, and impurity removal
definition: Compressing gas raises its temperature; since cold gas is denser than hot gas, cooling the gas after compression lets more gas mass be moved at a given pipeline pressure, and also reduces corrosion caused by trace impurities.
core_idea: Compressor stations cool gas after compression both to increase the effective transport capacity of the pipeline and to limit corrosion from the trace non-methane gases that are always present in natural gas.
key_points: Colder gas is denser, so at a constant operating pressure more gas can be transported if it is kept cool
Cooler gas causes less corrosion in the pipeline
Natural gas is never pure methane and always carries trace amounts of other gases, some of which are corrosive
Compressor stations include scrubbing systems to remove these trace impurities and particulates/liquids before compression, preventing mechanical breakdowns
relationships: Part of the compressor station process described above
caveats: Assuming compression is a purely mechanical pressure-boosting step with no thermal or gas-quality side effects
